title_en: The Thing I Want to Do Most
full_text_zh:
[P1] 最想做的事
[美] 玛莉·布雷比/文 [美] 克里斯·K·索恩皮/图 梅子涵/译

海豚绘本花园
湖北少年儿童出版社

[P3] 天没光——星星还在闪烁——爸爸、哥哥约翰和我，离开我们的小木屋，急忙上路，走出小镇去做工。

路的一边是卡纳瓦河，另一边是山。我们提着油灯，快步赶路。
我的肚子一直在咕噜咕噜叫，因为我们还没有吃早餐呢。不过，我真正想要的不是吃的东西，当然了，如果有得吃，那也很不错。

[P4] 我最想做的事是学会阅读。
可是现在，我必须做工。从日出到日落，
我们在盐场，把盐巴装进一只只木桶里。

[P5] 盐巴堆得像白色的山一样，比爸爸的个头还要高。我们整天铲着盐巴，盐山却一点儿也没变矮。

我们只有在吃饭的时候才休息一会儿——土豆和玉米饼是爸爸放在他的外衣口袋里带来的。我一边吃饭，一边看着这些白色的盐山。盐巴很重，也很粗糙。一不小心这些闪亮的白色晶体就会划破你的手、胳膊、腿和脚掌。

[P6] 因为整天举铁锹铲盐巴，我的手臂又酸又痛，但是我在意的不是这种痛，我想到的是心里对阅读的渴望，我看过别人阅读——有年轻人，也有老人。我已经九岁了。我知道，如果有机会，我也能阅读。

我想，那些书里一定藏着秘密。

晚上有点冷，我跟着爸爸和约翰一起回家。在路上，我抓到了一只青蛙。青蛙在我手里扭来扭去想要逃走，但是我抓得紧紧的。等我想放它走的时候，我才会松开手。

[P7] 我们生活的这个地方和以前有些不一样了，所有的人都可以去他们想去的地方，做他们想做的事情。我想学会阅读——这个想法就像鱼一样，在我脑子里自由地游来游去，我愿意想多久就想多久。

晚上回到镇上，煤矿工们、船夫们、樵夫们、桶匠们都围坐在角落里，他们和我一样疲惫，可是却一直说个没完。

[P8] 我看见一个人在大声地朗读报纸。顿时，我所有的疑虑都消失得无影无踪。我找到了希望，那个大声朗读的人和我一样，他的皮肤也是棕色的。

我在这个人身上看到了我的未来。我看到他的视线在报纸上移动，这时我好像也能看得懂那些黑色符号的意思，好像我也能阅读，好像每个人都正在听我朗读。想到这里，我紧紧握住了自己的手。

[P9] 我要努力成为本地最会阅读的人。小孩子们都会围着我，而我要教他们如何阅读。
但是，爸爸拍拍我的肩膀，约翰拉我的衬衫，说：“走吧。”
他们不明白我在想什么，他们也不知道我将会成为一个什么样的人。

[P10] 我们匆匆忙忙地回到家里。“妈妈，我一定要学会阅读！”我说。妈妈握住我的手，我想她一定能感觉到，我的渴望和我的心跳一样急迫。

[P11] 这是一本小书——颜色像夜空一样湛蓝。一天晚上，在我们小木屋的一角，妈妈把它从替人家洗烫的衣堆里抽出来，递给了我。
她没有说书是从哪里来的。她不会阅读，但是她知道这是一些被叫作“字母”的东西。她想，这可能是用来唱歌的，是印在纸上的一首歌。

[P12] 下工后，虽然肩膀还很酸痛，腿上还沾着盐巴，我仍然要看我的书。我凝视着那些符号，想象着它们的发音。

[P13] 我把那些符号画在地上，猜想它们应该怎么读，表示什么意思。
但是，有时候我觉得自己像一个没有腿的人，却在认真地跳跃。我
学习阅读的想法会溜走，我不能坚持下去实现自己的愿望。如果我能
学会这件美妙的事，那该有多好啊，人们会多么尊重我啊！
可是我想象不出这些符号的音调，我感觉到矿盐巴留下的酸痛，
我觉得我的梦想正在慢慢溜走。
我必须找到他——那个朗读报纸的人。

[P14] 我到处寻找。
终于，我看到了那张带给我希望的棕色脸庞。

[P15] 他教我唱这首“歌”——那些符号的发音。
我跳上跳下地唱着，我又喊又笑，就好像在小溪边接受洗礼一样。我已经跳进了另一个世界里，我得救了！

[P16] 但是我还想知道更多。“请多告诉我一些吧！”我说。
“你叫什么名字？”他问。
“布克。”我说。
他按照发音，把我的名字写在地上。

[P17] 我沉浸在这幅美景里，不舍得离开。我知道，我能永远握住我的梦想了。
full_text_en:
[P1] The Most Wanted Thing to Do
[US] Mary B. Brayby / Text [US] Chris K. Thornpie / Illustrations Mei Zihang / Translator

Dolphin Picture Book Garden
Hubei Children's Publishing House

[P3] It's not yet light—the stars are still twinkling—Dad, my brother John, and I leave our little log cabin, hurrying out of town to go to work.

One side of the road is the Kanawha River, the other side is the mountain. We carry oil lamps and walk quickly.
My stomach is rumbling, because we haven’t had breakfast yet. But what I truly want isn’t food. Of course, if there were food, that would be nice too.

[P4] The thing I want to do most is learn to read.
But now, I must work. From sunrise to sunset,
we are at the saltworks, loading salt into wooden barrels.

[P5] The salt piles are as white as mountains, taller than Dad's head. We shovel salt all day, but the salt mountains never get any smaller.

We only get to rest for a little while when we eat—potatoes and cornbread that Dad brings in his coat pocket. I eat while watching these white salt mountains. The salt is heavy and rough. If you're not careful, these shiny white crystals will cut your hands, arms, legs, and feet.

[P6] Because I spend all day lifting shovels and scooping salt, my arms are sore and tired. But what I care about is not this pain—it's the longing in my heart to read. I've seen others reading—both young people and old. I'm already nine years old. I know that if I get the chance, I can read too.

I think those books must hold secrets.

It's a bit cold at night. I'm walking home with Dad and John. On the way, I catch a frog. The frog wriggles and tries to escape in my hand, but I hold on tight. I'll only let go when I'm ready to set it free.

[P7] The place where we live is a bit different now. Everyone can go wherever they want and do whatever they want. I want to learn to read—this thought is like a fish, swimming freely in my mind. I can think about it as long as I want.

When we return to town at night, the coal miners, boatmen, woodcutters, and barrel makers all gather in the corners. They are as tired as I am, yet they keep talking without stopping.

[P8] I saw a man reading a newspaper aloud. Instantly, all my doubts vanished. I found hope—the man reading aloud was just like me, his skin was brown too.

I saw my future in this man. I watched his eyes move across the newspaper, and suddenly I felt as if I could understand the meaning of those black symbols, as if I could read, as if everyone was listening to me read. At that thought, I clenched my hand tightly.

[P9] I want to become the best reader in the area. The children will gather around me, and I will teach them how to read.
But Dad pats my shoulder, and John pulls my shirt, saying, "Come on."
They don't understand what I'm thinking, and they don't know what kind of person I will become.

[P10] We hurried back home. “Mom, I must learn to read!” I said. Mom held my hand. I thought she could feel it—my longing and my heartbeat, just as urgent.

[P11] This is a small book—its color as deep blue as the night sky. One evening, in a corner of our little wooden house, Mom pulled it out from a pile of laundry she had washed and ironed for others, and handed it to me.
She didn’t say where the book came from. She couldn’t read, but she knew it was something called 'letters.' She thought it might be for singing, a song printed on paper.

[P12] After work, even though my shoulders were still sore and salt still clung to my legs, I still had to read my book. I gazed at those symbols, imagining the sounds they made.

[P13] I draw those symbols on the ground, wondering how to read them and what they mean.
But sometimes I feel like a person without legs, yet trying to jump earnestly. My
idea of learning to read slips away; I can't stick with it to fulfill my wish. If I could
learn this wonderful thing, how wonderful it would be, and how much people would respect me!
But I can't imagine the sounds of these symbols, and I feel the sour ache from the mine salt,
I feel my dream slowly slipping away.
I must find him—the man who reads the newspaper.

[P14] I searched everywhere.
Finally, I saw that brown face that brought me hope.

[P15] He taught me to sing this 'song'—the sounds of those symbols.
I jumped up and down, singing, shouting and laughing, just like being baptized by a stream. I had jumped into another world, I was saved!

[P16] But I wanted to know more. 'Please tell me more!' I said.
'What's your name?' he asked.
'Book,' I said.
He spelled it out, writing my name on the ground according to its sound.

[P17] I am immersed in this beautiful scene, reluctant to leave. I know, I can forever hold onto my dream.
full_summary_zh:
[P1] 本页为绘本《最想做的事》的封面，展示了一个戴着帽子、穿着条纹衬衫和背带裤的男孩，他低头凝视着手中的一幅小画，背景是砖墙。封面上标注了作者、绘者、译者及出版社信息。
[P2] 画面展示了一个男孩站在盐堆旁，手持铲子，旁边有一个木桶和简易棚屋，远处是绿色山丘和冒着白烟的工厂，天空晴朗。
[P3] 夜晚，男孩与父亲、哥哥提着油灯，从木屋出发赶路去工作，途中经过河流与山丘，男孩虽饿但更渴望的是其他东西。
[P4] 画面描绘了男孩和工人们在盐场劳作的场景，他们用铲子将盐装入木桶，背景是冒着白烟的工厂和山丘。文字表达了男孩渴望读书，但不得不从早到晚在盐场做工的现实。
[P5] 画面描绘了男孩和工人们在盐场劳作的场景，他们坐在木桶上休息并吃着简单的食物，背景是巨大的盐堆和远处的河流与工厂。文字描述了盐堆的庞大、工作的艰辛以及盐粒对身体的伤害。
[P6] 男孩在辛苦劳作一天后，内心依然渴望阅读，他回忆起看到别人读书的场景，并坚信自己有机会也能读书。回家路上，他抓到一只青蛙，紧紧抓着它，直到自己决定放它走。
[P7] 男孩在夜晚回到镇上，看到工人们围坐在一起聊天，虽然疲惫但依然交谈不休，他内心对阅读的渴望持续存在。
[P8] 夜晚，男孩在镇上看到一位黑人男子在油灯下大声朗读报纸，深受鼓舞，仿佛看到了自己未来的可能性，内心对阅读的渴望更加坚定。
[P9] 男孩在夜晚看到一位黑人男子在油灯下朗读报纸，深受鼓舞，内心渴望成为会阅读的人并教导他人，但父亲和哥哥催促他离开，周围人并不理解他的梦想。
[P10] 男孩在夜晚回到家中，向母亲坚定地表达自己一定要学会阅读的愿望，母亲握住他的手，感受到他内心的急切与渴望。
[P11] 男孩在家中收到母亲递来的一本蓝色小书，母亲虽不识字，但知道书上有‘字母’，并认为它可能是用来唱歌的。
[P12] 男孩在辛苦工作后回到家中，尽管身体疲惫且腿上还沾着盐，他仍坚持在油灯下阅读，凝视书中的符号并想象它们的发音。
[P13] 男孩在油灯下于地上画出字母，努力学习阅读，但因无法想象发音而感到沮丧，梦想似乎正在溜走，他决心找到那位朗读报纸的人寻求帮助。
[P14] 男孩在夜晚的镇上四处寻找，终于找到了那位曾朗读报纸、带给他阅读希望的黑人男子。
[P15] 男孩找到了那位在油灯下朗读报纸的黑人男子，对方教他朗读书上的符号，男孩兴奋地跳跃欢呼，仿佛进入了一个全新的世界，内心充满喜悦与希望。
[P16] 男孩向那位在油灯下朗读报纸的黑人男子请教，男子询问他的名字并按照发音将“布克”写在地上，男孩对此充满期待。
[P17] 男孩在油灯下凝视着地上写下的名字，脸上洋溢着满足与希望，他确信自己能永远抓住梦想。
